The best souvenir is perspective. After staffing mobile clinics in Costa Rica, organizing cultural exchange conferences across Asia, and teaching in Taiwan, this past month of immersion in Chengdu (hosted by LTL Language School ) has been my favorite trip to date. A Chinese word captures it better than I could in English: 丰富 (fēngfú). It means rich, not financially, but in depth and abundance. Think: enriching relationships and perspectives that make your life feel full. I was initially introduced to 丰富 by my teacher, Pan Pan, who is only a few years my senior. Between grammar lessons and listening exercises, we found ourselves talking about how history and current events can differ so dramatically depending on where you grew up. Meanwhile, I’d have meals with classmates from the Netherlands, Mexico, Spain, and Brazil. Each had their own reason for learning Chinese: ambassadorship work, a company they were founding in Suzhou, or to decipher the language’s beauty. Beyond the school, those 丰富 perspectives extended to locals I met incidentally: the street vendor who explained different regional varieties of zongzi, or the calligraphy master who taught me Sichuan dialect. Through them, I realized language learning runs on compassion: to understand a culture, you’re striving to see it through someone else’s eyes. Before I arrived, I'd heard no shortage of stereotypes about mainland China. My own dad called me every day to make sure I was safe in the country. What greeted me in Chengdu was the opposite: overwhelming hospitality, warmth, and community. A month earlier, ordering takeout felt intimidating. By the end, I was confidently explaining to a hairstylist how I wanted my perm. Chengdu taught me that 丰富 is a lived experience as much as a mindset. I hope to carry that compassion into every patient interaction as I begin my journey in medicine.

Honored to be featured in the inaugural Harvard in Tech Builders interview! Huge thanks to Alicia Broggi and Nicole Soltau for the thoughtful questions and for putting together such a wonderful piece. In the interview, I share reflections on my journey as a startup founder building CodeYam , my experiences as a Harvard University alumna, and how my time at Harvard helped shape my approach to leadership, problem-solving, and building new things. While I often default to the TL;DR version of my experiences when asked, I took this as an opportunity to be honest and open about both the exciting and difficult parts of my journey. Building a company challenges you in countless and unexpected ways, and I've learned a lot from embracing uncertainty, vulnerability, and owning my experiences, including both the successes and the setbacks. Grateful to be part of such an inspiring community of builders and technologists, and looking forward to reading future Builder spotlights and learning from the incredible alumni featured next.

This was my view when I found out I'd been accepted to the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) School of Medicine. I was solo-traveling China. My first stop? The Chengdu Panda Research Base. I opened the email alone, thousands of miles from family, friends, and mentors. In that moment, I renewed a quiet promise to myself about the kind of doctor I wanted to be: one who cared for patients beyond treating symptoms. From countless attendings, residents, and medical students, the consensus on making the most of my last summer of freedom is always: "Live your life. Don't do anything medicine-related." Well… I hope this is a good middle ground. I'm going back to Chengdu to learn Mandarin in three weeks. Okay... not exactly. The real story is that I took a year of Mandarin at Harvard College, then promptly went on a forgetting curve. Then I found myself in rural Taiwan, in a town famous for our taro fields, for my English Teaching Assistantship with The Fulbright Program . For months, I relied on Google Translate, survival Mandarin, and a lot of body language just to get by. I met the most hospitable people, but struggled to connect further because of the language barrier. Though I'll admit there's something humbling about having your tones corrected by 6th graders, daily. So this summer, I'm partnering with LTL Language School for three weeks of full immersion. The goal isn’t fluency but foundation. A skill I can carry into medical school, and one day use to connect with my patients. Where better to start than Chengdu. 🐼

Last weekend, I ran my first 24K trail race in Colorado Springs. Then, because my race tracking failed and I’m apparently very stubborn, I ran another half marathon the next morning to earn NYRR Brooklyn Half virtual race credit. Then I climbed the Manitou Incline, which I’d known about since spending a summer at the Olympic Training Center in Colorado Springs nearly 17 years ago, but had somehow never attempted. Now that my legs have recovered a bit, I’ve had a chance to reflect on the experience and my stubbornness. Stubbornness often gets framed as a negative trait, but in the right contexts, I think it can be a superpower. The same stubbornness and grit that gets me through endurance experiments also shows up in startup founder life. I wrote about trail running, questionable decisions, supportive strangers, and what this all made me realize about myself. Full thoughts here: https://lnkd.in/gYqZqrqK

There are far too many people to thank individually, but just to name a few — Daniel Kim , Radvilas Pelanis , and Emma Phan — I’m especially grateful for your guidance, encouragement, and time along the way. Looking forward to summer 2027!

I am incredibly grateful for the unwavering support of my family, friends, mentors, and professors at the University of Pennsylvania , without whom this would not have been possible.
